analysis.one_liner: Gives consumers the right to freeze their credit files and bans bureaus from using Social Security numbers.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to its Banking Committee on October 18, 2017 and never acted on it again; it died when the 115th Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write a national right to a 'security freeze' into the Fair Credit Reporting Act. A freeze blocks the three big credit bureaus from releasing your credit report to open new credit in your name — the main tool against identity thieves who apply for loans using your stolen information. You could place, lift, or remove a freeze by phone or online, with the bureau acting within days. The bill also bars the nationwide credit bureaus from putting your Social Security number in any credit report or using it to identify you.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially identity theft victims, seniors over 65, minors, and active-duty service members, who would get a uniform national right to lock down their credit files.

how_it_helps.text: Consumers could demand a security freeze from any nationwide credit reporting agency, which blocks the bureau from releasing the consumer's report to anyone trying to open new credit in their name; a freeze stays in place until the consumer removes it.

Bureaus would have to place a freeze within 5 business days of the request and lift or remove one within 3 business days, with requests accepted by mail, phone, fax, or online, and the consumer gets a PIN or password to control it.

The fee is capped at $5 per freeze, lift, or removal, and identity theft victims with a police report, consumers who are minors or 65 or older, and active-duty service members with their orders pay nothing.

Nationwide credit bureaus could no longer include a Social Security number in any consumer report or use a consumer's Social Security number to identify them, effective January 1, 2020 — a direct response to how a stolen SSN lets fraudsters open accounts.

Bureaus would have to notify a consumer in writing before changing key file information like name, date of birth, Social Security number, or address, with address changes confirmed to both old and new addresses.

analysis.who_pays: The three nationwide credit reporting bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion), which face a new obligation to honor freezes at a capped fee and must strip Social Security numbers out of their reports; consumers not in the exempt groups pay up to $5 per freeze action.

drawbacks.text: A freeze is not free for most people under this bill: up to $5 each time you place, lift, or remove one, which adds up for someone shopping for a mortgage or applying at several lenders and then re-freezing afterward.

The list of exceptions is broad — current creditors and their affiliates reviewing accounts, insurance underwriting, employers, landlords, debt collectors, and courts can still see the file — so a freeze does not wall off your data completely, only new-credit inquiries.

A freeze can slow legitimate borrowing: bureaus get 5 business days to place one and 3 to lift it, and the bill's own required notice warns consumers that a freeze may delay credit, mortgage, rental, and job applications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real, meaningful protection for consumers against new-account identity fraud, at a modest price and some friction for lenders. The main weakness is the fee: most consumers would pay up to $5 per freeze action rather than getting it free, and the broad exceptions mean the freeze stops fewer things than people might assume. It would have been a genuine upgrade over the patchwork of state freeze laws, but a weaker deal for consumers than a free national freeze.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up; it expired when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator David Perdue introduced the bill on October 18, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No cosponsors signed on — zero, for the life of the bill.
The action history shows nothing after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action. The bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The three nationwide credit bureaus — no national freeze mandate and no Social Security number ban was imposed on them during that Congress, and they kept whatever fee and data practices the existing patchwork of laws allowed.

for.name: Sen. David Perdue
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PROTECT Act of 2017 in the Senate on October 18, 2017.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction; Chair Mike Crapo (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 18, 2017 and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Republican, ever sponsored the bill and no cosponsors joined, so the record shows no test of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill forces them to honor consumer freezes at a capped $5 fee within fixed deadlines and bans them from using or including Social Security numbers — a core identifier their databases are built around. The bill's entire value to consumers is the cost it imposes on this industry's control over credit files.

New-credit applications require the applicant to lift a freeze, adding days and possible fees to loan processing. On the other hand, freezes cut down on fraudulent accounts, which lenders otherwise absorb as losses.
